RagShortTexts: Votadinian communities maintained contacts beyond Rome's provincial frontier.
Traprain finds do not alone establish a specific treaty or royal constitution in 374.

Variants.Content: The module's Votadinian faction draws on communities around south-eastern Scotland, beyond the Roman provincial frontier. Sites such as Traprain Law show long-lived centres and contact with the Roman world, but finds do not by themselves prove a permanent treaty, a precise royal succession or a feudal court in 374. Local leadership can be described through settlements, kin, exchange and the capacity to provide protection. Neighbours may disagree over how closely to deal with Roman authorities and how to distribute the costs of guarding routes. Later Gododdin traditions and early fifth-century silver deposits must not be treated as eyewitness records of this opening year.

A man watching an upland approach needs to recognise familiar drovers and notice strangers before they reach the settlement. Trade with the south may bring valued goods, but guarding it takes time from animals and fields. A dispute between leaders matters when it closes a route or leaves a household without the help it expected.

A Votadinian notable gains influence from people and connections he can sustain, not from a later heroic genealogy alone. Roman objects may display access to exchange, yet say little about a particular agreement's terms. He must balance outside opportunities with the protection and supplies his own neighbours expect him to arrange.
